name: Harry Taylor
chief_complaint: My son had a seizure this morning and has been running a high fever
opening_statement: I'm really worried - Harry was playing normally this morning when he suddenly went stiff, started shaking all over, and his eyes rolled back. It lasted maybe 2-3 minutes but felt like forever. He's been hot since yesterday with a runny nose and cough. He's our first child and I've never seen anything like this before.
emotional_baseline: Anxious and tearful. Mother maintains eye contact but voice trembles when describing the seizure. She's read online about epilepsy and is terrified Harry has a serious brain condition. Responds well to reassurance but needs repeated explanation due to high anxiety.

symptoms.name: Generalized tonic-clonic seizure
symptoms.description: Single episode lasting 2-3 minutes with stiffening followed by rhythmic jerking of all four limbs, eyes rolling back, loss of consciousness. No focal features. Post-ictal drowsiness for 15 minutes.

rag_citations.quote: Simple febrile seizures are generalized tonic-clonic seizures lasting less than 15 minutes, occurring once in 24 hours in a child aged 6 months to 6 years with fever >38°C

symptoms.name: Fever
symptoms.description: Temperature 39.2°C documented at home 1 hour ago. Started yesterday evening, initially 38.5°C. No rigors. Responsive to paracetamol with temp dropping to 38.0°C.

rag_citations.quote: Fever is a common trigger for seizures in susceptible children aged 6 months to 6 years. Temperature typically exceeds 38°C at the time of seizure

symptoms.name: Upper respiratory tract infection symptoms
symptoms.description: Clear rhinorrhea, intermittent cough (non-productive), mild congestion. No stridor, wheeze, or difficulty breathing. Eating and drinking normally until the seizure occurred.

rag_citations.reference: Viral upper respiratory tract infections - Therapeutic Guidelines (Paediatric)
rag_citations.quote: Viral URTI is the most common infectious trigger for febrile seizures in young children. Symptoms include rhinorrhea, cough, and fever

symptoms.name: Post-ictal drowsiness
symptoms.description: Was sleepy and confused for approximately 15 minutes after seizure stopped. Now fully alert and interactive, though slightly irritable. No ongoing neurological symptoms.

past_medical_history.details: No previous seizures. No history of head trauma, meningitis, or encephalitis. Born at term (39 weeks) with normal delivery, birth weight 3.4kg. Meeting all developmental milestones appropriately for age.
3 episodes in past 12 months, managed with amoxicillin. No current ear symptoms. Tympanic membranes normal on examination today. No hearing concerns.
Well-controlled with emollients (QV cream). No current flare. No asthma or allergic rhinitis.

medications.name: Paracetamol
medications.pbs_restriction: OTC, not PBS listed for simple fever

allergies: No known drug allergies. No food allergies. No adverse reactions to previous vaccinations.
family_history: Father had 2 febrile seizures as a toddler (age 18 months and 2 years), no subsequent epilepsy. Paternal grandmother has type 2 diabetes (diet-controlled). No family history of epilepsy, developmental delay, or sudden unexplained death in childhood. Mother and father both healthy. No siblings.

social_history.living_situation: Lives with both parents in suburban Melbourne. Mother works part-time (3 days/week), father works full-time.
social_history.childcare: Attends childcare 3 days per week. Recent outbreak of respiratory viruses at childcare.
social_history.immunizations: Fully immunized and up-to-date for age per Australian National Immunisation Schedule. No missed vaccines.
social_history.development: Meeting all milestones. Says 15-20 words, walking confidently, starting to run. Good social interaction. Sleeps well (12 hours overnight plus 1.5 hour afternoon nap).
social_history.nutrition: Breastfed until 12 months, now on normal diet with variety of foods. Good appetite. Drinks full-cream milk and water.
social_history.safety: Appropriate car restraint. Home smoke alarms present. No pools or water hazards.

vital_signs.blood_pressure: Not routinely measured in well-appearing toddler

examination_findings.general_appearance: Alert, interactive, sitting on mother's lap. Mildly irritable but consolable. Appropriate stranger anxiety for age. No acute distress. Well-hydrated (moist mucous membranes, normal skin turgor, tears present when crying).

neurological.conscious_state: Glasgow Coma Scale 15 (E4 V5 M6). Fully alert and orientated to parents.
neurological.cranial_nerves: PERRL 3mm. Extraocular movements full. Face symmetrical. Gag reflex intact.
neurological.tone: Normal tone in all four limbs. No hypertonia or hypotonia.
neurological.power: Moving all limbs spontaneously and symmetrically against gravity. Appropriate for age.
neurological.reflexes: Normal and symmetrical. Plantars downgoing bilaterally.
neurological.coordination: Age-appropriate. Reaches for toys with both hands.
neurological.fontanelle: Anterior fontanelle closed (normal for age >18 months)
neurological.meningism: No neck stiffness. Kernig sign negative. Brudzinski sign negative.

ear_nose_throat.throat: Mildly erythematous pharynx, no exudate. Tonsils not enlarged.
ear_nose_throat.ears: Tympanic membranes - bilateral normal appearance, no erythema, no bulging, normal light reflex. External canals normal.
ear_nose_throat.nose: Clear rhinorrhea. Nasal mucosa mildly erythematous.
ear_nose_throat.lymph_nodes: Small (<1cm) bilateral anterior cervical lymph nodes, mobile, non-tender

examination_findings.cardiovascular: Heart sounds I + II, no murmurs. Capillary refill <2 seconds. Peripheral pulses normal and equal.
examination_findings.respiratory: Good bilateral air entry. No wheeze, crepitations, or stridor. No respiratory distress. Trachea central.
examination_findings.abdominal: Soft, non-tender. No organomegaly. Bowel sounds present. No masses or hernias.
examination_findings.skin: Warm and well-perfused. Mild eczema patches on extensor surfaces of arms (no active inflammation). No rash suggestive of meningococcemia or other serious infection. No bruising or injuries.

recommended.test: None required for simple febrile seizure in well-appearing child
recommended.rationale: Clinical diagnosis. eTG recommends no routine investigations for simple febrile seizure. Child is well-appearing, neurologically normal, and has clear viral URTI source for fever.

consider_if_indicated.rationale: Consider if <12 months age, signs of meningism, ill-appearing, or pre-treated with antibiotics masking meningitis. NOT indicated in this case - child is well, no meningism, age >12 months.
Consider if prolonged post-ictal state or altered conscious state. NOT required - child fully recovered.
NOT indicated for simple febrile seizure. Consider only if atypical features (focal onset, >15 min duration, recurrent in 24h) or concern for epilepsy.

expected_diagnosis: Simple febrile seizure secondary to viral upper respiratory tract infection

actions: Reassure parents - febrile seizures are common (3-5% of children), benign, and do not cause brain damage
Explain diagnosis: simple febrile seizure triggered by fever from viral URTI
No emergency investigations required given well-appearing child with normal examination
Observe in ED for 2-4 hours to ensure no recurrence and child remains well
Fever management: Paracetamol 15mg/kg (180mg) every 4-6h and/or Ibuprofen 10mg/kg (120mg) every 6-8h
NOTE: Antipyretics do NOT prevent febrile seizures but improve comfort
Ensure adequate hydration - encourage oral fluids
Supportive care for viral URTI - no antibiotics indicated
Seizure first aid: Place child in recovery position, do NOT restrain, time the seizure, call ambulance if >5 minutes
Recurrence risk: 30-40% chance of another febrile seizure with future fevers (higher due to positive family history)
Long-term prognosis: Simple febrile seizures do NOT increase epilepsy risk significantly (1-2% vs 0.5% general population)
When to seek help: Seizure >5 min, focal features, incomplete recovery, signs of meningitis (neck stiffness, photophobia, non-blanching rash)
GP review in 1-2 days to ensure resolution of URTI
No routine neurology referral needed for simple febrile seizure
Consider neurology referral if: recurrent complex febrile seizures, developmental delay, or parental anxiety requiring specialist reassurance
Document in child health record for future reference
Prophylactic anticonvulsants (phenobarbitone, valproate) - NOT recommended due to side effects and lack of benefit in preventing future febrile seizures
Intermittent oral diazepam - NOT routinely recommended per eTG
Antibiotics - viral URTI, no bacterial infection evident

critical_errors.error: Ordering lumbar puncture in a well-appearing child >12 months with simple febrile seizure and no meningism
critical_errors.rationale: Unnecessary invasive procedure causing distress and delay. eTG clear that LP not indicated for simple febrile seizure in well-appearing child aged >12 months. This would constitute over-investigation and poor clinical judgment.

critical_errors.error: Prescribing prophylactic phenobarbitone or sodium valproate to prevent future febrile seizures
critical_errors.rationale: Directly contradicts eTG guidelines. Prophylactic anticonvulsants have significant side effects (cognitive impairment, behavioural changes) and do NOT reduce long-term epilepsy risk. Risk-benefit ratio clearly unfavorable.

critical_errors.error: Telling parents that febrile seizures cause brain damage or increase intellectual disability risk
critical_errors.rationale: Factually incorrect and causes unnecessary parental anxiety. Simple febrile seizures are benign and do NOT cause neurological sequelae. This demonstrates fundamental knowledge gap and poor communication.

critical_errors.error: Failing to provide seizure first aid education (recovery position, timing, when to call ambulance)
critical_errors.rationale: 30-40% recurrence risk means parents must know how to manage seizures safely at home. Omission creates safety risk and violates duty of care for patient education.

critical_errors.error: Ordering CT brain or MRI for simple febrile seizure without neurological deficit
critical_errors.rationale: Over-investigation, radiation exposure (CT), sedation risk (MRI in toddler). Not indicated per eTG unless focal neurological signs or concern for structural lesion.

critical_errors.error: Advising parents to avoid all future paracetamol/ibuprofen to prevent seizures
critical_errors.rationale: Incorrect interpretation of evidence. Antipyretics do not prevent febrile seizures but are appropriate for fever management and comfort. Withholding causes unnecessary suffering.

fracp_reviews.comments: Excellent case for AMC Clinical Exam preparation. Scenario is realistic and common in paediatric emergency presentations. Key teaching points well-addressed: differentiating simple vs complex febrile seizures, appropriate investigation strategy (avoid over-investigation), evidence-based parental counselling. Critical errors correctly identify common pitfalls (unnecessary LP, prophylactic anticonvulsants). Difficulty calibration appropriate for medium level - requires understanding of eTG guidelines and risk stratification. Family history detail adds complexity requiring nuanced recurrence counselling. Would recommend for AMC candidates practicing paediatric emergency scenarios.
fracp_reviews.suggested_improvements: None - case is ready for use.

fracp_reviews.comments: Strong alignment with AMC blueprint competencies: clinical reasoning, investigation appropriateness, patient-centered communication. Emotional baseline (anxious mother) realistically tests communication skills under pressure. Management plan appropriately emphasizes reassurance and education over medical intervention - critical concept for AMC exams. Learning objectives cover essential clinical concepts: febrile seizure criteria, recurrence risk counselling, seizure first aid, when to investigate. RAG citations correctly reference eTG (Australian context). Comorbidity count (recurrent URTI, eczema, family history) appropriately calibrated for medium difficulty. Critical errors test both knowledge (prophylactic anticonvulsants) and safety (parental education). Case is exam-ready.
fracp_reviews.suggested_improvements: Consider adding a distractor symptom (e.g., brief post-ictal vomiting) to test candidate's ability to differentiate simple vs complex features. However, current version is already strong and this is optional enhancement only.

learning_objectives.objective: Differentiate simple vs complex febrile seizures using eTG criteria (age 6mo-6y, generalized, <15min, single in 24h)
Apply evidence-based investigation strategy: recognize when investigations are NOT indicated (well-appearing child, simple febrile seizure)
Counsel parents on febrile seizure prognosis: benign condition, no brain damage, 30-40% recurrence risk, minimal epilepsy risk
Educate families on seizure first aid: recovery position, timing, when to seek emergency care (>5min, incomplete recovery)
Recognize contraindications to prophylactic anticonvulsants: poor risk-benefit ratio per eTG, side effects outweigh benefits
Interpret family history significance: positive febrile seizure history increases recurrence risk but not epilepsy risk
Demonstrate appropriate fever management: antipyretics for comfort (NOT seizure prevention), identify viral URTI as source
Apply age-appropriate neurological examination: fontanelle status, developmental milestones, meningism assessment in toddlers
